items.prompt: Define globalisation.
items.canonical_answer: Globalisation is the growing integration of the world's economies, in which businesses source, produce and sell across national borders and goods, services, money and people move between countries more freely than before.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must include the integration of the world's economies through cross-border business activity. "Businesses trading internationally" alone is not the full meaning.

items.prompt: Etosha Beads makes jewellery in Windhoek. Ten years ago it sold to Namibian tourists who visited the workshop; today it sells online to buyers in Europe and posts the parcels by air freight. Explain how the changes behind globalisation made this possible, and what the change has meant for the business.
items.canonical_answer: Condition: the starting point is the shift given - from selling to visiting tourists to selling online across borders. Mechanism: cheap worldwide communication lets European buyers find the workshop and pay it from abroad, and cheap reliable air freight carries the parcels, so distance no longer hides a small Namibian producer. Consequence for the business: the market has widened far beyond Namibian tourists, so sales and revenue can rise - though the business is now exposed to foreign demand and shipping costs it does not control.
marking_guidance: Condition: the chain must start from the given change, the move from tourist sales to online sales abroad. Mechanism: award for the how - cheap communication lets foreign buyers find and pay the business, because distance no longer hides it, and air freight moves the goods. Consequence: award for the effect on the business - a wider market and higher sales, with the new exposure as a second consequence.

items.prompt: Oshakati Spice Co. buys chilli from Namibian farmers, mills it in Otavi and sells to supermarkets in Namibia and Germany. Its owner says the business has become "part of globalisation". Explain what globalisation means for this business, using its facts, and what the owner should weigh before expanding the German side.
items.canonical_answer: The context facts show globalisation at work here: the business sources locally but sells across borders, so its market is no longer bounded by Namibia, and German supermarket shelves put it beside spice producers from anywhere in the world. The reasoning is that the same integration that widens its market also widens its competition, and foreign sales expose it to demand abroad and to the movements of the exchange rate between the Namibian dollar and the euro. Conclusion: the owner should weigh the larger German market against the exposure that comes with it - dependence on a foreign market it cannot control - before committing more resources to it.
marking_guidance: Context: award for using this business's facts - Namibian farmers, a Namibian mill, German supermarket customers. items.prompt: Explain the main reasons why globalisation has grown over recent decades.
items.canonical_answer: The main reasons come in four parts. Cheaper transport: container shipping and air freight carry goods between continents for a fraction of former costs. Cheaper communication: the internet lets buyers and sellers find, pay and track each other across any distance. Reduced trade barriers: governments have cut the duties and paperwork that once guarded national markets. And the pull of multinational networks: businesses spreading across borders draw their suppliers and retailers into worldwide chains. What the four include in common is the falling cost and friction of crossing borders, which is what integration means.
marking_guidance: Features: award one mark for each element - cheaper transport, cheaper communication, reduced trade barriers, the pull of multinational networks - and one mark for developing what the parts include in common.

items.prompt: Define an opportunity of globalisation for a business.

items.prompt: Explain why globalisation can be a threat to a small Namibian business.
items.canonical_answer: One reason is foreign competition arriving at home: imported goods can carry prices below what a small local producer's costs allow, because foreign makers often work at far greater scale, so the local business loses sales even though it has done nothing worse. A second reason is dependence: a small business that imports key materials or relies on foreign customers is exposed to events abroad - a shipping disruption or a slump in another country - that it cannot influence, and its smaller reserves make that exposure harder to survive.
marking_guidance: Reason: award for each reason developed with its because - foreign competitors can undercut a small firm's prices because of their scale, and dependence on foreign suppliers or customers exposes it to conditions it cannot control. Two developed reasons are needed for full credit.

items.prompt: Explain the features of the opportunities globalisation can offer to a business.
items.canonical_answer: The features come in three parts. A larger potential market: customers in many countries become reachable, so sales no longer depend on the home town. Cheaper or better inputs: a wider range of suppliers tends to lower costs or raise quality. Access to ideas and technology: seeing how producers elsewhere work spreads better practice quickly. What each opportunity includes is a condition - foreign sales depend on demand abroad holding up, and imported inputs depend on shipping behaving - so taking the opportunity also takes on exposure the business does not control.
marking_guidance: Features: award for each element - larger market, cheaper or better inputs, access to worldwide ideas - and for what it includes on the condition side: the exposure that comes with foreign sales and imports.

items.prompt: Okahandja Furniture Works employs 60 people making wooden chairs, but imported chairs arrive at prices its costs cannot match and its sales are falling. The owner welcomes a government proposal to place a tariff on imported furniture. Explain what a tariff would mean for Okahandja Furniture Works, and what the owner should weigh before counting on it.

items.prompt: Explain the features of import tariffs and import quotas as ways of restricting imports.
items.canonical_answer: A tariff's features are that it is a tax acting through price: every imported unit lands dearer, so the restriction is felt whenever buyers pay. A quota's features are that it is a physical limit acting through quantity: once the allowed amount is used up, imports stop for the period, whatever buyers would pay. What the two include in common is a deliberate restriction at the border, usually introduced to protect home producers and the jobs that depend on them, and both tend to raise the price of the good in the home market, which is the cost consumers carry for the protection.
marking_guidance: Features: award for each element - a tariff as a tax acting on price, a quota as a physical limit acting on quantity - and for what the pair includes in common: both act at the border to protect home producers and tend to raise home-market prices.

items.prompt: Explain the main benefits a business can gain from becoming a multinational.
items.canonical_answer: The main benefits come in four parts. Closeness to customers: producing inside a foreign market cuts transport and avoids the tariffs and quotas that stand at its border. Cheaper or better inputs: materials come from where they are abundant and labour from where it is skilled or lower-cost. Spread of risk: a drought, a strike or a slump in one country no longer threatens the whole business, because operations sit in several. Scale: production across several plants can support bulk buying and specialised equipment. What the benefits include together is a business less dependent on the conditions of any single country.

items.prompt: Explain the difference between appreciation and depreciation of a country's exchange rate.
items.canonical_answer: The distinction is the direction of the movement. Appreciation means one unit of the home currency buys more foreign currency than before, so foreign goods become cheaper to home buyers. Depreciation means one unit buys less, so foreign goods become dearer to home buyers. The boundary between them is the direction of what one unit buys abroad: more is appreciation, whereas less is depreciation. Seen from the foreign currency's side the same movement reverses - a depreciation of the Namibian dollar against the euro is an appreciation of the euro against the Namibian dollar.
marking_guidance: Distinction: award for the boundary - the direction of what one unit of the home currency buys abroad, more being appreciation, whereas less is depreciation - and for the mirror view from the other currency, so both sides of the pair are named.

items.prompt: Explain how a business that exports most of what it makes can benefit when its country's currency depreciates.
items.canonical_answer: A depreciation means foreign buyers need less of their own currency to pay the exporter's home-currency prices, so the business's goods become cheaper on foreign shelves. items.prompt: A learner writes: "Rundu Honey Farm became part of globalisation on the day it sent its first jars to customers in Botswana." Explain the error in this statement.
items.canonical_answer: The error is treating globalisation and selling abroad as the same thing. In fact exporting is one activity a single business chooses: Rundu Honey Farm decided to send jars across a border, and that decision belongs to the farm. Globalisation is an economy-wide process - the growing integration of the world's economies as transport and communication become cheaper and governments lower the barriers around national markets. It changes the conditions whole industries trade under, whether or not a particular business exports. Before its first shipment the farm was very likely affected already: imported honey may compete with its jars on Namibian supermarket shelves, and its jars, lids or labels may be bought from suppliers abroad. The test that tells them apart: ask whether the statement describes one business's decision or the conditions across a whole economy. The first shipment is a decision; globalisation is the set of conditions that made that shipment cheaper and easier to arrange. The farm took up an opportunity the process offered; it did not join the process on that day.
marking_guidance: The error is named and corrected: in fact exporting is one activity a single business chooses, while globalisation is an economy-wide process that affects businesses whether or not they export.

A 6-mark answer states what selling abroad is (one business's choice to sell across a border), states what globalisation is (the growing integration of the world's economies), and applies the test - one business's decision or economy-wide conditions? - to the honey farm's first shipment.

items.prompt: A learner writes: "Globalisation brings opportunities and threats to multinationals, but Keetmanshoop Bakery sells in one town, so globalisation does not affect it." Explain the mistake in this statement.
items.canonical_answer: The mistake is treating globalisation as something that happens to multinational businesses. In fact a multinational is one kind of business: it has its headquarters in one country and operations it controls in at least one other. Globalisation is not a kind of business at all; it is the economy-wide integration of the world's markets, and its opportunities and threats can reach a business that never crosses a border. Keetmanshoop Bakery may face a threat as imported biscuits and cakes arrive on the town's supermarket shelves at prices its own costs struggle to match, and it may gain an opportunity by buying flour, ovens or packaging from a wider range of suppliers abroad. Its dependence on imported inputs is a further exposure to events it cannot control. The test that tells them apart: ask whether the statement is about where a business owns its operations, or about the conditions businesses across the economy trade under. Being a multinational is the first; globalisation is the second, so the bakery's single location does not place it outside the process.
marking_guidance: The error is named and corrected: in fact a multinational is one kind of business with operations in more than one country, while globalisation is an economy-wide process whose opportunities and threats can reach a business operating in one town.

A 6-mark answer states what a multinational is, states what globalisation is, identifies at least one opportunity or threat that reaches the bakery, and applies the test - where the business operates, or the conditions it trades under? - to the statement.

items.prompt: A learner writes: "To protect local cement makers, the government has introduced a legal control: imported cement now carries an extra tax when it crosses the border." Explain the error in this statement.
items.canonical_answer: The error is calling a trade restriction a legal control. In fact a tax placed on goods as they enter the country is an import tariff. A tariff, like its partner the import quota - a limit on the quantity that may be brought in over a period - acts at the border: it changes what may enter the country and at what price. Legal controls act somewhere else. They are laws that regulate how businesses operate inside the economy, such as pollution limits, safety standards and employment law, and they bind a business whoever owns it and wherever its products come from. The confusion is understandable because both are made by government and backed by law; the difference is where the rule bites. The test that tells them apart: ask whether the rule acts on goods as they cross the border or on how a business behaves inside the country. An extra tax on imported cement acts at the border, so it is a tariff, introduced to protect home producers by raising the price of imports. A rule limiting the dust a cement kiln may release would be a legal control, and it would apply to the local makers themselves.
marking_guidance: The error is named and corrected: in fact a tax on imported goods at the border is an import tariff, a trade restriction, not a legal control on how businesses operate inside the economy.

A 6-mark answer states what an import tariff (or quota) is and where it acts, states what legal controls are and where they act, and applies the test - does the rule act at the border or inside the economy? - to the tax on imported cement.

items.prompt: A learner writes: "When Okavango Tyres opened a second factory in Zambia, the stakeholders affected were its shareholders, because stakeholders are the people who own the business." Explain the mistake in this statement.
items.canonical_answer: The mistake is treating stakeholders and shareholders as the same group. In fact shareholders are the owners of a company: they hold shares, may receive dividends and vote on major decisions. They are one stakeholder group. Stakeholders are the wider set of groups affected by the business's decisions - workers, customers, suppliers, lenders, governments and local communities - whether or not they own a single share. Opening the Zambian factory affects far more than the owners. The shareholders gain the chance of higher profits but carry more risk. Workers at the Namibian plant may see some roles move to the new site, while Zambian workers gain jobs. Suppliers near each plant may win or lose orders, and the two governments may gain or lose tax revenue. The test that tells them apart: ask whether a group holds a financial ownership stake in the business or a stake in what the business does. A shareholder holds both kinds of stake; a worker, supplier or community holds the second without the first, and is still a stakeholder.
marking_guidance: The error is named and corrected: in fact shareholders are the owners of a company and are one stakeholder group, while stakeholders include every group affected by the business's decisions, such as workers, suppliers, customers and governments.

A 6-mark answer states what shareholders are, states what stakeholders are, applies the decision to at least two non-owning stakeholder groups, and gives the test - ownership stake or a stake in what the business does? - applied to the Zambian factory.

items.prompt: A learner writes: "The Namibian dollar has appreciated against the euro, so Luderitz Fish Exporters will find it easier to sell its fish in Spain." Explain the error in this statement.
items.canonical_answer: The error is reversing the direction of the change: the learner has given an appreciation the effect of a depreciation. In fact an appreciation means one Namibian dollar now buys more euros than before. Seen from Spain, the same movement means each euro buys fewer Namibian dollars, so a Spanish buyer needs more euros to pay the exporter's Namibian-dollar price. Luderitz Fish Exporters' fish therefore tends to become dearer in Spain, which is likely to make it harder, not easier, to sell there - unless the business accepts a lower price in Namibian dollars to hold its euro price, or its buyers value the fish's quality and reliability enough to pay more. A depreciation works the other way: each Namibian dollar buys fewer euros, Namibian goods become cheaper for Spanish buyers, and exporters tend to gain orders. The same appreciation tends to help a Namibian importer, because goods priced in euros cost fewer Namibian dollars. The test that tells them apart: ask what one unit of the home currency now buys abroad - more is appreciation, less is depreciation - then follow which way the payment flows.
marking_guidance: The error is named and corrected: in fact an appreciation makes Namibian exports dearer for foreign buyers, so it tends to make exporting harder; easier exporting is the tendency that follows a depreciation.

A 6-mark answer states what appreciation means (one unit of the home currency buys more foreign currency), states what depreciation means (it buys less), explains the effect of the appreciation on the exporter's price abroad with its conditions, and gives the test - what does one Namibian dollar now buy abroad? - applied to the statement.

items.prompt: The manager of Tsumeb Textiles, a clothing maker with 40 workers, watches imported garments arrive at prices below its own costs of production. Some of its cotton fabric is imported. Write several linked points for the manager: state two threats globalisation brings to this business and one opportunity it could pursue, each with a reason, and close with what you recommend for this business.
items.canonical_answer: Threat one: imported garments priced below its production costs, because foreign makers operate at far greater scale, so the business loses sales however well it produces. Threat two: dependence on imported fabric, because shipping costs and currency movements abroad reach its costs directly. Opportunity: selling distinctive Namibian designs online to a wider market, because globalisation makes foreign customers reachable at almost no cost. Recommendation: for this business, moving upmarket into designs the imports do not copy is likely to work better than a price fight it cannot win, while the online market spreads its sales beyond the home shelves - and the manager should check what share of costs the imported fabric carries before assuming the exposure is large.
marking_guidance: Point: award for each point stated - two threats and one opportunity, up to the tariff of the task. Reason: award for the because behind each point - scale advantages, imported-fabric exposure, reachable foreign customers. Context: award for applying each point to this business - its 40 workers, its costs, its imported fabric - rather than writing in general terms.

items.prompt: Kalahari Beverage Group, a multinational headquartered in South Africa, plans a juice plant near Otavi: N$40 million of investment, 300 jobs at the plant, and 70 per cent of output exported. Three local juice makers, employing 90 people between them, already serve Namibian shops, and the plant will import its packaging. Using the facts, consider whether the Otavi area should welcome the plant.
items.canonical_answer: Judgement: on balance, yes - provided conditions hold. The context facts: 300 direct jobs and N$40 million of investment arrive against 90 people employed in existing local makers, and 70 per cent of output exported would earn foreign money for the area, while consumers gain another choice on the shelves. The criterion that decides it is whether the new jobs are net jobs: if the plant's scale and brand take supermarket contracts from the three local makers, some of the 90 existing jobs go, and the gain is smaller than it looks. The counterargument: the plant imports its packaging, so local suppliers gain little beyond fruit, and profits may be repatriated to South Africa rather than reinvested in Otavi - the host keeps the jobs while much of the financial return leaves. Recommendation: welcome the plant, conditional on local-sourcing contracts for fruit and a commitment to reinvest profits locally; unless those conditions are agreed, the drawbacks could eat the gains.
marking_guidance: Judgement: award for a clear recommendation on the plant. Context: award for using the facts - 300 jobs against 90, the N$40 million investment, the 70 per cent exported, the imported packaging. Criterion: award for naming what decides it, such as whether the new jobs are net jobs after losses at existing makers. Counterargument: award for the case against welcoming - sales taken from local makers, packaging imported, profits repatriated. Condition: award for the recommendation depending on stated conditions, such as local-sourcing contracts and reinvestment.

items.prompt: Plan, without writing the full answer, a response to this 12-mark task: "A country usually gains more than it loses when a multinational locates there." Consider this view. Set out the paragraphs you would write, the judgement you would reach and the criterion that decides it, the case against your judgement, and the conditions your recommendation would depend on.
items.canonical_answer: Plan. Paragraph 1, define the terms: what a multinational is, and what "gains" and "losses" mean for a country - jobs, exports, choice and investment on the gain side; lost sales for local businesses and repatriated profits on the loss side. Paragraph 2, the case for the view: jobs at the plant and among local suppliers, export earnings, wider choice, and investment in capacity the country need not fund itself. Paragraph 3, the case against: local businesses can lose sales and shed jobs; repatriation of profits sends the financial return to the home country; and a plant that can arrive can also leave. Paragraph 4, judgement: the view holds where local sourcing and reinvestment are real - the criterion is whether the jobs and spending stay in the country and whether existing firms survive the competition. Recommendation conditional on: the share of the plant's spending that goes to local suppliers, whether profits are reinvested, and the strength of existing local firms.

Criterion: the plan must name what decides the verdict, such as whether jobs and spending stay in the country. Counterargument: the plan must include the case against the view. items.prompt: Walvis Bay Wetsuits sews diving suits from neoprene imported from Germany and sells three-fifths of its output to Namibian dive shops, the rest to buyers in Europe. Over the past year the Namibian dollar has appreciated against the euro. Analyse the position this leaves the business in and recommend what the owner should do.
items.canonical_answer: Analysis: the appreciation cuts both ways for this business. Where it pays - imported neoprene priced in euros - each Namibian dollar now buys more, so its material cost falls and margins on every suit improve. Where it is paid - European sales - its Namibian prices translate into more euros for foreign buyers, so its suits have become dearer abroad, and European customers may drift to rivals whose costs sit in currencies that have not moved. The criterion that decides the position is the balance between the two: imported materials are a large share of each suit's cost, while European sales are two-fifths of output, so the net effect is likely to help margins overall but to slow the export side. Counterargument: if the European buyers are price-sensitive, the export sales could be lost altogether, and the home market is not guaranteed to absorb them. Recommendation: hold foreign prices where possible and use the cheaper neoprene to protect the margin on each export sale, while looking for materials at home or in currencies that have moved differently - conditional on whether European orders hold; unless they do, the business may need to lean further on its Namibian customers.
marking_guidance: Judgement: award for a clear recommendation for the owner. Context: award for using the facts of the business - imported German neoprene, three-fifths of sales at home, the appreciation against the euro. Criterion: award for naming what decides it, the balance between cheaper imported materials and dearer exports. Counterargument: award for the case against relying on the net gain - price-sensitive European buyers may be lost. Condition: award for the recommendation depending on stated conditions, such as European orders holding and alternative sourcing.
